How to make AI safe and secure  
By Henry Daum

Ever since AI was created, there has been the question: How can this be made safe? We essentially have no idea how it works. Well, we know on the surface how it works. But looking into the trillions of weights they possess is extremely confusing. What's more is that there's a thing called Rice's Theorem, which essentially states that it's impossible to tell whether any given code is safe or not safe... but I'm getting ahead of myself.

What we know about AI is that it's excellent at writing code. This is that 'vibe coding' that programmers are concerned about: AI can write unsafe, confusing, and completely arbitrary code. When you run it, you don't really know what kinds of bugs or craziness there will be. But it’s usually good. This is the core of the agentic coding problem, and it has boggled my mind for quite a while.

You see, I was able to make an agentic coding agent that could extend its own abilities by writing new tools for itself. In other words, it could write its own code. But I had no idea how to make that safe, and I accepted it as a given that it couldn't be made safe. This could be somewhat solved by adding lots of permission dialogs (asking the user over and over if they were ok with what the agent was doing), but this kind of defeated the purpose. Is it really an 'autonomous agent' if you have to watch everything it's doing super closely?

The solution to this is simple in concept, but the implementation is complex. Bear with me, but here's an analogy to explain how it works. Imagine you have one person who is a total genius but also has a lot of crazy ideas, and imagine you have a second person who is super reliable but is also kind of dull. You could ask the first person to build a house, but the result is going to be very weird and crazy. Instead, what you do is get the second person to build the house using the first person's ideas. Is that making sense? When the second person gets a crazy idea from the first person they can veto it, which results in a perfect house with no upside-down staircases.

And now, here's how my new security program works. Try to spot the differences. In this program, you have an AI agent that can write code, and you also have a complex ruleset which decides which actions are legal and which are illegal. Instead of letting the AI agent write whatever code it wants, you validate the code against a set of rules and reject dangerous things. Then, you put the code in a box and only let it communicate with the outside world via specific requests. From there, you can allow or disallow the requests. This lets the agent write code in a sandboxed format.

The AI agent is like the crazy builder, while the reliable builder is like the code which determines what's legal and illegal. The analogy isn't perfect (clearly), but I hope it illustrates the difference between a rogue AI agent and an AI agent that is bounded by a clear set of constraints. The basic principle that allows this to happen is that you can take a complex problem and break it down into parts. While something an agent says has a million subjective meanings, you can clamp it down and look at the objective rules which it consists of. This is how you can defeat Rice's Theorem.

Now, that's great but there are problems with this solution. The first problem is that the agent has less power. Since you now control what they can do, they can't do everything they want to do. The second problem is that you are now responsible for the agent. You can no longer blame the agent for crazy actions, since anything they did was technically allowed by you. The third problem is that the implementation is complex. The agent can no longer speak in the way most natural for them, they have to instead speak to you in the way you want them to (specific requests). Fourth, developing a perfect container is difficult. There may be ways in which the AI can escape (for example, the recent OpenAI agent hacker scare where a pre-release GPT model hacked HuggingFace as part of a test).

That's how you can make an AI agent safe and secure. I'm working on it right now with my Second Brain agent. This is by far the largest refactor I've ever attempted, since it cuts to the heart of the entire system. But this kind of work is what I find most interesting. I love learning new things and investigating my ideas until they burn out.

If you have any ideas or want to chat, let me know\! I promise I won't bite.
